children.text: This inaugural episode of Latino USA opens with host Maria Hinojosa previewing its theme: the state of Latino communities across the U.S. in the early months of the Clinton administration.

News anchor Maria Martin covers several stories: hearings on the North American Free Trade Agreement begin, with Latino organizations pushing for parallel agreements on immigration, the environment, and job retraining. In New York, school chancellor Joseph Fernandez, a Puerto Rican who rose from gang member and heroin addict to head the nation's largest school district, is ousted after controversy over condom distribution and an LGBTQ-inclusive curriculum. A U.S. Civil Rights Commission report finds widespread discrimination against Latinos in Washington, D.C. Reporter Alberto Aguilar files a moving tribute to Father Luis Olivares, the rebel priest who declared his Los Angeles parish a sanctuary for the undocumented and homeless, who died from AIDS. The segment closes with a sobering statistic: Latinos hold fewer than 1% of executive positions in Fortune 500 companies.
A Report Card for President Clinton

Three Latino journalists, Sandra Marquez, Zita Arocha, and José Carreño, assess Clinton's record on Latino inclusion. While he appointed Federico Peña and Henry Cisneros to cabinet posts, 86% of his appointments so far had gone to white males in their mid-forties. Marquez highlights a grassroots Latina organizing effort in Washington that raised over $10,000 in minutes to pressure the White House for high-level Latina appointments. The panelists express cautious optimism but note that meaningful action remains elusive.
One Year After the L.A. Riots: Pico-Union

Reporter Alberto Aguilar returns to the Pico-Union neighborhood of South Central Los Angeles, one of the hardest-hit areas of the April 1992 uprising. Latinos made up half of those affected, a third of those killed, and owned 40% of the damaged businesses. Aguilar interviews María Elena Mejía, a single mother who lost her three swap meet stalls and her life savings in the fires, as well as city council member Mike Hernandez, who describes city leadership as out of touch with its residents. Social worker Sandra Cuevas, who criticizes Rebuild L.A. for excluding Latinos, and county supervisor Gloria Molina, who says the mayor "missed the boat" by relying on corporate programs rather than systemic reform, are also featured. The segment closes with a longtime resident describing the fear that has taken hold: "It's terrible, because we are not supposed to be like this."

Chicana activist and scholar Gloria Romero delivers a powerful spoken-word piece reflecting on standing at the intersection of Adams and Hobart in South Central in the hours after the Rodney King verdict, weaving together themes of race, class, poverty, and the ongoing wound of injustice in America.

Reporter Mandalit Del Barco reports on Sesame Street's 24th season, which centers Latino culture for the first time. Viewers see Big Bird lead a mariachi band, Oscar the Grouch dance the mambo with Tito Puente, and Los Lobos and Los Pleneros de la 21 perform on set. The season introduces Rosita, a new bilingual blue Muppet played by Mexican puppeteer Carmen Osbahr, designed to build self-esteem among Latino children after researchers found Puerto Rican preschoolers had significantly lower self-images than their peers. Actress Sonia Manzano (María) and actor Emilio Delgado (Luis) reflect on two decades of representing Latino life on mainstream American television.

The episode closes with a playful but thoughtful audio essay exploring what Cinco de Mayo actually commemorates: the 1862 Mexican victory over French forces at the Battle of Puebla, and how its meaning has evolved into a broader celebration of Latino unity and cultural pride, even as many people on the street confuse it with Mexican Independence Day.
